verdicts.note: No abstract; precarious employment and uncertain futures in Japan. Fifth country chapter of the youth-transitions volume.
Kin support modifying the opportunity cost of BREASTFEEDING. A.13's outcome, with the extended arm's mechanism.
No abstract; digital life and second-child fertility behaviour in CFPS. C.2.h's.

Encyclopedia entry on GRANDPARENTING, summarising how grandparental childcare relates to younger generations' fertility decisions and labour force participation. The C.2.a literature's own summary of the boundary this chapter routes against.

No abstract; SPILLOVER EFFECTS OF RURAL PENSION on a CHILD'S MARRIAGE DECISION, China's NRPS. The same pension-policy variation as the batch-16 discontinuity, now with a downstream family-formation outcome rather than the arrangement. Trace.
Juvenile justice under Lampung customary law.
No abstract; FAMILY STRUCTURE, orphanhood and adolescent SEXUAL DEBUT AND MOTHERHOOD across Africa and Asia. Both axes named; the configuration and the direction are not visible. Trace.

'EXTENDED FAMILY STRUCTURES EXERT A CAUSAL INFLUENCE ON FERTILITY' -- and it names the gap this chapter's extended arm sits in: the alloparenting literature concentrates on the mother's parents and parents-in-law, while the fertility impact of EXTENDED FAMILY STRUCTURE itself has had much less attention. A causal claim on exactly the registered estimand. Priority read and priority scrutiny.

Three-generation KIN DISPERSION as a spatial process in the nineteenth-century US, and it criticises exactly what the proximity cell's other records do: most historical studies rely on SNAPSHOTS of co-residence or proximity within a single moment. A dynamic treatment of the exposure.
No abstract; childlessness and sonlessness and wellbeing in older Indian adults.
Declining consanguinity in Pakistan's Potohar Plateau.

'PARENTAL HOMES AS FEATHERED NETS: HOME-LEAVING TRAJECTORIES OF YOUNG PEOPLE IN CHINA' in Socius, arguing the STAY/LEAVE DICHOTOMY is inadequate for prolonged, REVERSIBLE and complex transitions, especially in East Asia where intergenerational co-residence is a long-standing norm. This is §9's measurement problem stated as the paper's premise, in the setting where both configurations coexist. Priority read.

No abstract; the SHIFTING NATURE of intergenerational co-residence in South Korea 1975-2020. A 45-year series on the exposure in a key setting; 'shifting nature' suggests the construct-change warning the Japanese record raised.
Commentary on family law in Israel.
Supplementary file for the Russian emerging-adulthood study.
Projection model treating childlessness as structural rather than attitudinal.
Living arrangements and depression among elderly Chinese.
Determinants of reverse mortgage enrolment in Korea.
Demographic wellbeing across post-Soviet states.

'FROM LEAVING HOME TO PARENTHOOD': how SIBLING relationships change across household and family formation, noting the transition out of the parental home has had scant attention. The chain is the frame; the outcome is the sibling bond.
Essays on gender, demography and human capital.
No abstract; One-Child Policy, female schooling and intergenerational transfers in general equilibrium.

'FAMILY-ANCHORED' TRANSITIONS TO ADULT LIFE IN MEXICO: young adults commonly CO-RESIDE WITH OWN PARENTS OR OTHER EXTENDED FAMILY WHEN FORMING A FIRST PARTNERSHIP OR BECOMING A PARENT, and the authors say the practice has scarcely been studied. That is a configuration neither §6 value covers -- the birth happens INSIDE the parental household rather than after leaving it -- and it dissolves the assumed ordering that §3 is built on. Priority read; likely a scope amendment.
Children's family pathways from birth to age ten in the UK.

INTERGENERATIONAL TRANSMISSION OF HOME-LEAVING PATTERNS, using intergenerationally linked SHARE data to relate parents' home-leaving ages to their children's. A pre-determined parental exposure acting on the arrangement -- and the parent's own age at leaving is a candidate instrument the scope never enumerated. Priority read.
Cooking energy use in Chinese homes.
OLG model of ageing, pensions and growth.

Demographic reconstruction of early modern Wurzburg covering every life stage from infancy through LEAVING HOME, marriage and fertility. Pre-modern; A.7's under Ruling 2, but it has the whole sequence in one reconstitution.
Review and research agenda on SIBLINGS AND SCHOOL PEERS in young adults' life-course events, against the known parental influences. Names a channel the scope treats only through parents.
Young people in South Korea under a changing age structure and very low fertility, including opportunities for labour market entry and leaving home.
Dataset for the post-industrial parenting-village study of childrearing support.
No abstract; sharenting and children's privacy.
Family size and food allergy in Japanese children.
No abstract; delayed retirement, intergenerational childcare and equilibrium fertility in an OLG model.
Allomothering and childrearing support in urbanised ultra-low-fertility societies. C.2.a's exposure with an evolutionary frame.
CO-RESIDENCE WITH CHILDREN and number of children against intergenerational support among rural older adults in Guangxi.
Retrofitting outdoor space in Chinese communities with intergenerational overlap and grandparental childcare.
Emotional closeness and conflict with PARENTS-IN-LAW by parenthood and relationship duration. Relationship quality as outcome.
Proxy framework for estimating Chinese GDP.
Duplicate of the Chinese GDP proxy paper.

THE ONLY EXPERIMENT IN THE FRAME. A 2x4 FACTORIAL SURVEY EXPERIMENT with difference-in-differences on how PARENTAL RETIREMENT DELAY affects adult children's FERTILITY INTENTIONS in China, against the 2025 statutory retirement-age rise. C.2.a owns the exposure, but randomised variation on this mechanism exists nowhere else in the frame and the design is one the extended arm could adapt to co-residence directly.
Elderly dependence and intergenerational support in Vietnam, including co-residence.
Clinical review of single parenting.
Pregnancy stress among Chinese women with a second child.
No abstract; socioeconomic disparities in the child penalty in China.

'THE IMPACT OF HOUSEHOLD STRUCTURE ON FERTILITY: A STUDY IN VIETNAM' in Demographic Research: nine years of panel data on 1,200 households with a FIXED EFFECTS model to control unobserved household factors. Panel fixed effects on this chapter's exact estimand -- the cleanest observational identification strategy in either arm, because it differences out the time-invariant selection into co-residence that §3 warns about. Priority read.

LIVING ARRANGEMENT TRAJECTORIES of young MEXICAN women by cohort and social stratum, explicitly against prior work that documented isolated events. Trajectory rather than event, in a Latin American setting; pairs with the family-anchored transitions record above.
Psychosocial experience of hybrid work.

CORESIDENT GRANDPARENTS and the Asian-white maternal employment gap in the US, opening on the point that fertility and employment decisions are linked and both depend on childcare availability. The exposure IS co-residence rather than care, so it is the extended arm's variable -- but the estimated outcome is employment.
Health of female former prisoners.
Sociological rather than psychological treatment of the EMPTY NEST, criticising the dichotomous framing of prior work. The parents'-side construct, now with a literature critique attached.
Loneliness predicting nursing home placement.

Marriage and childbearing intentions among unmarried employed young adults in SEOUL through a SOCIAL EXCLUSION framework, Seoul Young Adult Panel. The pre-launch population and a fertility-intention outcome; whether the arrangement is among the exclusion measures needs full text.
Firearm storage in households with children.

LIVING ARRANGEMENTS and women's HOUSEHOLD DECISION-MAKING POWER in China, explicitly correcting a literature that focused on nuclear families and OVERLOOKED THE PARENTS' ROLE. The bargaining mechanism the extended arm's fertility records invoke, measured directly; outcome is power, not births.
